quote: Theorem 2.2. The equality LµX (t) = LµY (t) holds for all 0 < t < τXY if and only if µX (t) = c µY (t) for all 0 < t < τXY , for some constant c > 0.
family: lifetime distributions with positive continuous MRL
compared: equality of MRLAI functions of two rvs

hypotheses.text: positive continuous MRLs on common support

conclusion.direction: LµX ≡ LµY iff µX = cµY (proportional MRL) — MRLAI equality up to MRL scaling

ambiguity: Basis for preorder/antisymmetry discussion of ≤MRLAI in Section 4 (p40).

quote: Theorem 2.4. Let X be a continuous lifetime random variable having M RLAI function LµX . If LµX (t) is independent of t for all t over the support X, then the support cannot be finite. Further, if LµX (t) = c for all t ∈ (0, ∞), then the distribution of X is exponential and conversely.

conclusion.direction: LµX ≡ c forces c = 1 and exponential; exponential ⇒ LµX ≡ 1

ambiguity: Contrast: constant FRAI characterizes Weibull (Nanda et al.), while constant MRLAI characterizes exponential.

quote: Theorem 2.5. Let X be a random variable defined on [0, τX ]. If µX is nonincreasing on [0, τX ), then LµX (t) ≤ 1 for all 0 < t < τX . The converse is not necessarily true. [counterexample: µX = 1−0.4t on [0,2), 0.1t on [2,3), 0.3 on [3,∞), giving non-monotone LµX < 1]

conclusion.direction: X DMRL ⇒ LµX(t) ≤ 1; converse false (piecewise-linear µX counterexample, Fig 1a)

ambiguity: Embedded counterexample shows DMRLA \ DMRLAI exists.

quote: Theorem 2.6. Let X be a random variable defined on [0, τX ]. If µX is nondecreasing on [0, τX ), then LµX (t) ≥ 1 for all 0 < t < τX . The converse need not hold. [counterexample: µX = 1+t on [0,5), 11−t on [5,6), 5 on [6,∞), non-monotone LµX > 1]

conclusion.direction: X IMRL ⇒ LµX(t) ≥ 1; converse false (Fig 1b)

ambiguity: Embedded counterexample gives IMRLA \ IMRLAI.

quote: Theorem 2.8. Let X have a positive continuous M RL function on the support [0, τX ). Then X ∈ DM RLA if and only if LµX (t) ≤ 1 for all 0 < t < τX , and X ∈ IM RLA if and only if LµX (t) ≥ 1 for all 0 < t < τX .
compared: characterization of DMRLA/IMRLA classes via MRLAI ≤/≥ 1

conclusion.direction: DMRLA ⇔ LµX ≤ 1; IMRLA ⇔ LµX ≥ 1

quote: Theorem 2.9. Let X have a positive continuous M RL function µX on the support [0, τX ). Then X is DM RLAI if and only if AX is geometrically concave. Similarly, X is IM RLAI if and only if AX is geometrically convex.
compared: structural characterization of DMRLAI/IMRLAI via geometric concavity of A_X(t) = ∫0^t µX

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI ⇔ AX geometrically concave (log A_X(e^y) concave); IMRLAI ⇔ convex

quote: Theorem 2.10. Let X have finite positive mean and a positive continuous M RL function on [0, τX ). If X is DM RLAI (resp. IM RLAI), then LµX (t) ≤ (resp. ≥) 1 for all 0 < t < τX . ... Combining Theorems 2.8 and 2.10, we obtain DM RLAI ⊊ DM RLA and IM RLAI ⊊ IM RLA.
compared: class inclusions DMRLAI ⊊ DMRLA, IMRLAI ⊊ IMRLA

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI ⇒ LµX ≤ 1 ⇒ DMRLA; strict inclusions DMRLAI ⊊ DMRLA and IMRLAI ⊊ IMRLA

ambiguity: Strictness witnessed by Theorems 2.5/2.6 counterexamples.

quote: Theorem 2.11. Assume that µX is differentiable and positive on the support (0, τX ). Then X is DM RLAI (resp. IM RLAI) if and only if LµX (t) ≥ (resp. ≤) 1 + tµ′X (t)/µX (t), 0 < t < τX .
compared: characterization of DMRLAI/IMRLAI via pointwise inequality

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI ⇔ LµX ≥ 1 + tµ′X/µX; IMRLAI ⇔ ≤

ambiguity: Remark 2.3: with Thm 2.10 gives DMRLAI ⊊ DMRL (Erlang f(t) = t²e^{−t}/2 counterexample: L(2.5)≈0.7767, L(5)≈0.7525, L(10)≈0.7721 non-monotone) and IMRLAI ⊊ IMRL.

quote: Theorem 2.12. Let {Xθ : θ > 0} be a proportional hazards family with survival functions F̄θ (t) = {F̄0 (t)}θ , 0 ≤ t < τ0 , and let H0 (t) = − log F̄0 (t). If H0 is positive and differentiable on (0, τ0 ), then Lθ (t) = L0 (t), 0 < t < τ0 . Hence, the F RAI function is invariant under the proportional hazards family.
compared: FRAI invariance across the PH family

conclusion.direction: Lθ(t) = L0(t) for all θ — FRAI constant across proportional hazards

ambiguity: MRLAI is NOT invariant in the PH family — see Counterexample 2.1.

quote: Counterexample 2.1. Consider the Weibull family F̄θ (t) = e−θt^α , t ≥ 0, α > 1, θ > 0. Since Hθ (t) = θtα , we have Lθ (t) = tHθ′ (t)/Hθ (t) = α, t > 0, so the F RAI function is independent of θ. ... for θ1 ≠ θ2 , [µθ1/µθ2 limits unequal] hence µθ1 and µθ2 are not proportional. Therefore, by Theorem 2.2, Lµθ1 ≢ Lµθ2 . Thus, equality of the F RAI functions does not imply equality of the corresponding M RLAI functions.
compared: FRAI equality vs MRLAI equality across proportional hazards

conclusion.direction: Lθ1 = Lθ2 (FRAI equal) but Lµθ1 ≢ Lµθ2 — FRAI equality ↛ MRLAI equality

quote: Example 2.1. Let X have the Pareto type II survival function F̄X (t) = (1 + t/β)−α , t ≥ 0, α > 1, β > 0. ... assumptions of Theorem 2.7 are satisfied with ρ = 1. Moreover, LµX (t) = 2(β + t)/(2β + t) → 2 = 1 + ρ as t → ∞.

conclusion.direction: LµX(t) = 2(β+t)/(2β+t) → 2; µX regularly varying index ρ = 1

quote: Example 2.2. Consider a random variable having the M RL function µX (t) = 1 + t/2 (0 ≤ t ≤ 1), t + 1/2 (t > 1). Then LµX (t) = (4+2t)/(4+t) (0<t≤1), 4t²+2t over 2t²+2t+1 (t>1) which is increasing in t > 0. ... LX (0.99) ≈ 0.8234, LX (1.01) ≈ 1.0879, LX (2) ≈ 0.7149, the F RAI function is non-monotone.

conclusion.direction: X is IMRLAI (LµX increasing) but FRAI non-monotone — IMRLAI ↛ IAI

quote: Example 2.10. Consider a lifetime random variable X with M RL function µX (t) = 1 + t (0≤t≤1), (5 − t)/2 (1<t≤2), 3/2 (t>2). ... quote: Example 2.11. Suppose a lifetime random variable X has survival function F̄X (t) = exp{−t − t2 /2}, t ≥ 0. LX (t) = (3/2)t^{3/2}/[(1 + t^{3/2}) ln(1 + t^{3/2})] which is strictly decreasing in t. So, the distribution belongs to the DAI class. LX (t) = t(1 + ln(1 + t))/[(1 + t) ln(1 + t)] ... the F RAI function LX (t) is non-monotone, attaining a maximum near t ≈ 5, while the M RL function µX (t) is strictly decreasing.
compared: non-monotone FRAI with strictly decreasing MRL (DMRL)

Let X1 and X2 be i.i.d. lifetime random variables with common M RL function [piecewise: 2 (0≤t≤5/2); 2−(3/125)(t−5/2) (5/2<t≤5); (97/125)(15/2−t) (5<t<15/2)]. ... each component belongs to the DM RLAI class. Now, let X1:2 = min{X1 , X2 } ... Figure 13(b) shows that LµX1:2 (τX x) is non-monotone. Hence, the DM RLAI class is not closed under the formation of a series system.

quote: Theorem 3.1. Let n ≥ 1, and let X1 , . . . , Xn be i.i.d. absolutely continuous lifetime random variables over the support with common differentiable survival function F̄X , and M RL function µX (t) = a + bt, 0 ≤ t < τX , where a > 0 and b > −1. If X1:n = min{X1 , . . . , Xn }, then LµX1:n (t) = LµX (t), 0 < t < τX .
family: linear-MRL family µX = a + bt, a > 0, b > −1
compared: MRLAI invariance under series-system formation within linear-MRL family

hypotheses.text: Xi iid, µX = a + bt, a > 0, b > −1

conclusion.direction: LµX1:n ≡ LµX — series system preserves MRLAI function exactly; DMRLAI/IMRLAI preserved within linear-MRL family

The survival function of Xc is F̄Xc (t) = (t + 1)e−t , whereas ... µXc (t) = (t + 2)/(t + 1). Then ... DM RLAI class is not closed under convolution.

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI NOT closed under convolution (also used for IMRLAI, since exponential is both)

Consider now X with survival function F̄X (t) = 0.2(8t + 1)−9/8 + 0.8(0.1t + 1)−11 ... Figure 14 shows that LµX (t) is non-monotonic. Consequently, the IM RLAI class is not closed under mixture.

Thus each component belongs to the IM RLAI class. ... X1:2 = min{X1 , X2 } ... Numerical integration gives LµX1:2 (1) ≈ 1.5577, LµX1:2 (4) ≈ 1.5778, and LµX1:2 (25) ≈ 1.5649. Thus LµX1:2 (t) is not nondecreasing. Hence, the IM RLAI class is not closed under the formation of a series system.

quote: Example 4.1. Let Xi , i = 1, 2, have Pareto type II survival function F̄Xi (t) = (1 + t/βi )−αi , αi > 1, βi > 0, t ≥ 0. If β1 ≥ β2 , then X1 ≤M RLAI X2 .
compared: MRLAI order between two Pareto-II variables by scale β

conclusion.direction: X1 <=MRLAI X2 for β1 >= β2

ambiguity: LµXi(t) = αi(βi+t)/(αiβi+t)? — recorded as printed (ordering in β).

quote: Theorem 4.1. For two lifetime random variables X and Y , X ≤M RLAI Y if and only if AX (t)/AY (t) is nonincreasing on (0, τXY ).
compared: characterization of the MRLAI order via the cumulative-MRL ratio

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y iff AX/AY nonincreasing (equivalently LµX ≤ LµY pointwise)

ambiguity: Proof omitted as easy. Later text (p40): ≤MRLAI is a preorder; antisymmetric only under common right endpoint, common initial MRL, no atom at 0.

quote: Theorem 4.2. Let X and Y have positive continuous M RL functions on (0, τX ) and (0, τY ), respectively. If µX (t)/µY (t) is nonincreasing on (0, τXY ), then X ≤M RLAI Y .
compared: sufficient condition for MRLAI order via MRL ratio

conclusion.direction: µX/µY nonincreasing ⇒ X <=MRLAI Y

ambiguity: Sufficient condition; note µX/µY nonincreasing is the MRL-order condition, so ≤mrl ⇒ ≤MRLAI direction via this theorem — but cf. Counterexamples 4.2/4.5 showing non-equivalence (X ≤MRLAI Y without X ≤mrl Y, and lr without MRLAI).

quote: Theorem 4.3. Let X and Y have positive continuous M RL functions on (0, τX ) and (0, τY ), respectively. Then, for each fixed 0 < a < τXY , Xa ≤M RLAI Ya if and only if [AX (a + s) − AX (a)]/[AY (a + s) − AY (a)] is nonincreasing on (0, τXY − a).

conclusion.direction: Xa <=MRLAI Ya iff increment ratio [AX(a+s)−AX(a)]/[AY(a+s)−AY(a)] nonincreasing

quote: Corollary 4.3.1. Let X and Y have positive continuous M RL functions on (0, τX ) and (0, τY ), respectively. If µX (t)/µY (t) is nonincreasing on (0, τXY ), then Xa ≤M RLAI Ya for every 0 < a < τXY .
compared: preservation of MRLAI order under residual lifetimes — sufficient condition

conclusion.direction: Xa <=MRLAI Ya for every age a — only sufficient (Counterexample 4.1 shows X <=MRLAI Y can fail to persist to Xa <=MRLAI Ya)

ambiguity: Sufficiency only — see Counterexample 4.1.

quote: Counterexample 4.1. Let Y be an exponential random variable with mean one. Then µY (t) = 1 and LµY (t) = 1 for all t > 0. Let X have the M RL function µX (t) = 1 − 0.4t (0≤t<2), 0.1t (2≤t<3), 0.3 (t≥3). ... Hence LµX (t) < 1 = LµY (t) for all t > 0, and therefore X ≤M RLAI Y . Now consider the residual lifetimes at age a = 2. ... LµX2 (s) = (4 + 2s)/(4 + s) > 1 = LµY2 (s), 0 < s < 1. Consequently, X2 ≰M RLAI Y2 , although X ≤M RLAI Y .

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y but X2 ≰MRLAI Y2 — MRLAI order not preserved under residual lifetimes in general

quote: Counterexample 4.2. Let X be an exponential random variable having failure rate 0.5, and let Y be another random variable having survival function F̄Y (t) = (t + 1)−3 . Then, we have LµX (t) = 1 and LµY (t) = 2(t + 1)/(t + 2), for t ≥ 0, so that X ≤M RLAI Y . However, X ≰icx Y since ∫t^∞ F̄X − ∫t^∞ F̄Y = 2e−t/2 − 1/[2(t + 1)2 ] [= 0.6802033 at t = 2; −0.001138222 at t = 18]. Moreover, µX (1) = 2 > µY (1) = 1, and hence X ≰mrl Y .

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y but X ≰icx Y and X ≰mrl Y — MRLAI does not imply icx or mrl

numbers: tail-integral difference 0.6802 at t=2, −0.00114 at t=18; µX(1)=2 > µY(1)=1

quote: Counterexample 4.3. Let X have survival function F̄X (t) = (t2 + 2t + 2)e−t /2, and let Y have Pareto survival function F̄Y (t) = (t + 1)−3 , t ≥ 0. ... It can be verified that LµX (t) ≤ LµY (t) for all t > 0, so that X ≤M RLAI Y . Next, define b(t) = [∫t^∞∫u^∞ F̄X ]/[∫t^∞∫u^∞ F̄Y ] = (t + 1)(t2 + 6t + 12)e−t . Then b(0.40) = 13.66380, b(0.80) = 14.10533, and b(1.5) = 12.96944. Since the ratio required for the vrl order is 1/b(t), and 1/b(0.40) > 1/b(0.80), we have X ≰vrl Y .

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y but X ≰vrl Y

ambiguity: Note: text defines vrl via a double-tail-integral ratio; the required ratio 1/b(t) fails monotonicity.

quote: Counterexample 4.4. Let X and Y have Erlang densities fX (t) = 9te−3t and fY (t) = 4te−2t , t ≥ 0. Then F̄X (t) = (1 + 3t)e−3t and F̄Y (t) = (1 + 2t)e−2t . A direct calculation gives [double-integral ratio] = 3e^t (2t + 3)/[4(t + 1)] whose logarithmic derivative is 1 − 1/[(2t + 3)(t + 1)] > 0. Hence X ≤vrl Y . On the other hand, ... R(t) := [∫0^t µX ]/[∫0^t µY ] = 4{3t + ln(3t + 1)}/[9{2t + ln(2t + 1)}] ... R(0.1) = 0.653742 > R(1.5) = 0.628701 < R(5) = 0.637118, R(t) is not nonincreasing. Therefore X ≰MRLAI Y , showing that X ≤vrl Y does not imply X ≤M RLAI Y .

conclusion.direction: X <=vrl Y but X ≰MRLAI Y — the two orders are incomparable

quote: Counterexample 4.5. Let X and Y be two independent random variables having Erlang distribution with respective density functions fX (t) = 9te−3t , t ≥ 0 and fY (t) = 4te−2t , t ≥ 0. It is easy to see that X ⩽lr Y . However, [∫0^t µX]/[∫0^t µY] = 4{3t + ln(3t + 1)}/[9{2t + ln(2t + 1)}] = [0.65370 at t = 0.1; 0.6287006 at t = 1.5; 0.6371185 at t = 5]. Thus, we have X ≤lr Y does not imply X ≤M RLAI Y.

conclusion.direction: X <=lr Y but X ≰MRLAI Y — hence none of lr, hr, st, mrl, vrl, icx implies MRLAI

ambiguity: Corollary drawn in text: no classical order implies MRLAI; and MRLAI is not equivalent to mrl.

quote: Theorem 4.4. Let X and Y be lifetime random variables. If X is DM RLA and Y is IM RLA, then X ≤M RLAI Y .
compared: sufficient class condition for MRLAI order

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y

ambiguity: Sufficient only — Counterexample 4.6 (both IMRLA yet ordered).

quote: Counterexample 4.6. Let X and Y have M RL functions µX (t) = 1 + t and µY (t) = 1 + 3t, respectively, for t ≥ 0. Then LµX (t) = 2(t + 1)/(t + 2) and LµY (t) = 2(1 + 3t)/(2 + 3t), t > 0. Since LµY (t) − LµX (t) = 4t/{(t + 2)(3t + 2)} > 0 for all t > 0, we have X ≤M RLAI Y . However, both X and Y are IM RLA, showing that the sufficient condition in the preceding theorem is not necessary.

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y with both IMRLA — DMRLA-vs-IMRLA condition not necessary

quote: Corollary 4.4.1. If X is decreasing in M RL and Y is increasing in M RL then X ≤M RLAI Y .

quote: Theorem 4.5. Let {Xi , i = 1, . . . , m} and {Yj , j = 1, . . . , n} be two sets of independent and identically distributed random variables with M RL functions µXi (t) = a + bt and µYj (t) = c + dt, respectively, where a, c > 0 and b, d ≥ 0. Then the following statements hold. (i) Xi ≤MRLAI Yj if and only if ad − bc ≥ 0. (ii) If Xi ≤MRLAI Yj , then for all m, n ≥ 1, X(m) = min Xi ≤MRLAI Y(n) = min Yj .
compared: MRLAI order of linear-MRL components and of series systems built on them

quote: Theorem 4.6. Let X and Y be non-negative continuous random variables such that X ≤M RLAI Y . Then, for every a > 0, the M RLAI order is preserved under the transformation ϕ(x) = ax, that is, ϕ(X) ≤M RLAI ϕ(Y ).

conclusion.direction: aX <=MRLAI aY — order preserved under positive scaling

ambiguity: Does NOT extend to affine shifts ϕ(x) = x + b (Counterexample 4.8).

LµX (t) < LµY (t) for all t > 0, showing that X ≤MRLAI Y . Now, consider the affine transformation ϕ(x) = x + 2 ... The two functions cross at t = (8 + 2√226)/5, as illustrated in Figure 18.
